title: Eagles Hunted Baboons Much Heavier Than Themselves
summary: Imagine an eagle catching an animal almost seven times heavier than itself. Scientists think that is what happened in the Sahara Desert in Chad. Researchers found the remains of at least nine adult baboons that Verreaux's eagles had recently killed. These eagles swoop down from cliff tops. Their talons spread about 16 inches across, and marks on the bones show they were killed, not scavenged. The baboons were big. On average they weighed about 49 pounds, and the largest weighed 58 pounds. Until now, scientists thought eagles could not lift primates heavier than about 29 pounds. The new study, published on November 18, suggests that old limit was wrong. The find raises questions about our early human relatives. Lucy, who lived about 3.2 million years ago, weighed around 62 pounds. Catherine Hobaiter said several early human relatives could also have been in danger from eagles. Only one case is confirmed: the Taung Child, taken by a large eagle around 2.8 million years ago. Eight of the nine baboons were male, and scientists say that is still a puzzle.
why_it_matters: Learning how eagles hunted long ago helps us understand how early humans stayed safe from dangers in nature.

background_read: In the Sahara Desert in Chad, Verreaux's eagles hunt by swooping down from high cliffs and grabbing animals with their wide talons.
This time the eagles caught adult baboons much heavier than themselves, which surprised scientists who thought eagles could only take much smaller prey.
The find matters because early human relatives were about the same size as those baboons, so they may have faced the same danger from eagles.
